newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma imposes curfew in Mandalay after unrest.
newsitem.headline: Burma imposes curfew in Mandalay after unrest.

text.p: Burma's military government imposed a curfew and other restrictions on its second city of Mandalay following unrest blamed by a spokesman on people trying to destabilise the country.
Residents said Mandalay newspapers reported that martial law was also in place, but copies of the paper could not be obtained in Rangoon.
The government spokesman told Reuters the country's military rulers had imposed the curfew in parts of Mandalay following clashes between Buddhist monks and Moslems.
He did not respond to questions on martial law and diplomats said they could not confirm that it had been imposed.
"Curfew has been imposed in some townships in Mandalay to prevent a recurrence of such incidents," the spokesman said.

Residents in Mandalay said a curfew was imposed from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. in five townships, effective from Monday. They said barricades had been set up on some Mandalay streets and the main market was closed.
The spokesman said some Buddhist monks in Mandalay destroyed personal belongings in several houses and mosques after a young Buddhist girl was molested by a Moslem youth.
He gave no details but a diplomat said at least two mosques were destroyed and several people were wounded in the weekend attacks.
"My understanding is that there were riots on the 15th and 16th. It seemed to be more of a socio-religious problem than a political protest," said another diplomat.
The spokesman said the unrest appeared to be the work of people intent on destroying the stability of the nation.

"Some elements are exploiting the situation by trying to promote misunderstanding between the two religions. The main reason for this is to cause unnecessary problems for Myanmar (Burma) so that Myanmar's entry into ASEAN will face problems."

Burma hopes to be accepted this year as a full member of ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations), which at present grouyps Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

"The main reason for this tension...(is) to create unrest in the country by creating disturbances wherever and whenever opportunity arises, to create misunderstanding between Myanmar and her ASEAN friends, especially with Indonesia and Malaysia which are both Islamic nations," the spokesman said.
He said the unrest was part of a plan to create problems in Burma, starting with agitation by students, then by monks and eventually workers.
Thousands of students took to the street in December in rare demonstrations against the government. Since then, all major universities have been closed.
Mandalay is home to a large portion of the monks in Burma, where about 90 percent of the population is Buddhist.
Monks played a key role in pro-democracy uprisings from 1988-1990 and many were arrested after refusing to perform religious services for soldiers and their families.
Since then the monks have been largely silenced, partly through intimidation and in part through offerings given to top monks by the government.
But diplomats and analysts say there have been signs recently of unrest among younger monks who want to see a democratic Burma.
Opposition sources say support from monks would be crucial for major change to take place in Burma.
